evidence.excerpt: This chapter surveys quantitative cost-of-quality modelling approaches as applied to electronics assembly, tracing development from early PAF accounting frameworks through activity-based and process-cost models to more recent optimisation formulations. The authors examine the data structures required by each model class, practical obstacles to data collection in contract manufacturing, and the degree to which each approach has been validated against real production data rather than hypothetical examples. Particular attention is given to the treatment of batch-size variability, multi-stage inspection architectures, and the estimation of hidden failure costs—three characteristics that distinguish electronics contract manufacturing from the mass-production settings where most CoQ theory was originally developed. The chapter identifies several open problems: the absence of longitudinal studies tracking CoQ outcomes after model-guided interventions, limited integration with modern defect-traceability systems, and weak linkage between CoQ models and supply chain quality costs upstream of assembly. Directions for further empirical and modelling research are outlined.
